title: DIA-SPROX E.coli and S.cerevisiae Midpoints
projectDescription: The stability of proteins from rates of oxidation (SPROX) technique is a mass spectrometry-based approach for making protein folding stability measurements on the proteomics scale. The development and application of SPROX, to date, has involved the use of quantitative bottom-up proteomics and data dependent acquisition (DDA) strategies using isobaric mass tags. Use of isobaric mass tags is attractive as it enables the mass spectrometry readout in SPROX to be highly multiplexed. However, use of such isobaric mass tags is restricted to DDA strategies, which can be limited in their proteomic coverage compared to data independent acquisition (DIA) strategies. Reported here is a new “one-pot” SPROX workflow that employs a DIA readout and a label-free quantitation strategy. Analysis of the proteins in an E.coli cell lysate using our DIA-SPROX strategy allowed for calculating transition midpoints with reasonable accuracy. The proteins from a S.cerevisiae cell lysate were also assessed for ligand induced changes in their transition midpoints  upon the introduction of cyclosporine A (CsA) to identify protein targets of this well-studied ligand. Using DIA-SPROX, we successfully identified known protein targets of CsA with a low false positive rate using a combination of two different software, Spectronaut and DIA-NN, for DIA data processing. We also find that the proteomic coverage obtained using DIA-SPROX is comparable to the coverage obtained in conventional DDA-SPROX experiments. Significantly, this comparable coverage can be achieved without using a methionine-containing peptide enrichment strategy in DIA-SPROX.
sampleProcessingProtocol: One-Pot SPROX. Both the E.coli lysate and the (+) and (-) yeast ligand stocks were subjected to a one-pot SPROX analyses performed in triplicate. Aliquots containing 5 µg of total protein were combined with 10 µL of a series of PBS buffers containing 21 different GdmCl denaturant concentrations such that the final denaturant concentrations were evenly spaced between 0 M and 5 M by 0.25 M. The initial concentrations of GdmCl were determined by refractive index measurements as described previously.21 Lysates were incubated with denaturant for 2 hours at room temperature before treatment with 1.5 µL of 30% hydrogen peroxide. The oxidation reaction was allowed to proceed for 3 minutes before quenching with 125 µL of 1 M TCEP. For each denaturant series, equal amounts of protein from each GdmCl containing buffer were combined into one tube to make up the one-pot samples. Additional endpoint control samples prepared using PBS and final GdmCl concentrations of 0 M and 5 M were also generated by adding 85 µg of total protein to 170 µL of denaturant at 0 M and 7.5 M GdmCl. These samples were also subjected to a 3-minute oxidation reaction upon the addition of  25.5 µL of 30% hydrogen peroxide, before they were quenched with 2.125 mL of 1 M TCEP.   The one-pot and end-point control samples were placed in 10 kDa MWCO centrifugal filters and subjected to a FASP procedure as previously described.22 In the FASP procedure, protein samples are denatured in 8 M urea, treated with TCEP and MMTS to reduced and alkylate disulfide bonds, and digested with trypsin. Before LC-MS/MS analysis, samples were desalted using C18 Macrospin Columns and dried down by speed vac.    DIA LC-MS/MS Analysis. The prepared samples were analyzed on an Orbitrap Astral LC-MS/MS system from ThermoFishser. A total of 1 µg of protein was loaded onto Evotips, and samples were analyzed using an Evosep One LC interfaced to the Orbitrap Astral MS using a 30 sample-per-day method with a PepSep 15 cm/150 µm column (1.5 µm particle size) and a PepSep Sprayer with a stainless steel (30 µm) emitter. Data collection was performed in a DIA mode of acquisition with a resolution of 240,000 (@ m/z 200) full MS scan every 0.6 s from m/z 380-980 with an AGC target of 500%. DIA MS/MS scans were acquired in the Astral analyzer using fixed windows of 4 m/z from m/z 380-980, target AGC of 500% and max fill time of 6 ms. A normalized collision energy of 28% was used for all MS2 scans.
dataProcessingProtocol: The LC-MS/MS raw data was processed with Spectronaut 19 using a Uniprot E.coli or S.cerevisiae database appended with common contaminants. Search settings included trypsin specificity, peptide length of 7-52 amino acids, variable N-terminal protein acetylation and methionine oxidation, and fixed cysteine alkylation modifications. Each replicate of data was processed separately. Raw data was also processed using DIA-NN 2.0 using a Uniprot E.coli or S.cerevisiae database and common contaminant database and following the same search settings used in Spectronaut. Both software were used to process data using a library-free search method.  After processing, data was exported to Microsoft Excel, contaminant proteins were removed, and precursors were divided into non-methionine, WT methionine, and oxidized methionine containing peptides. The sums of all the non-methionine precursor ion signal intensities in each sample were used to generated a normalization factor relative to the individual peptide ion signal intensities from the 0 M GdmCl control sample. For the S.cerevisiae data, each CsA(+/-) replicate was normalized to the CsA(+) 0 M GdmCl control sample. This normalization factor, which adjusts for any differences in overall protein concentration from sample to sample, was used to adjust the ion intensities of the individual methionine-containing peptides in each sample. After the above normalization, precursors with one methionine residue and no acetyl modifications were used for subsequent analyses. To get peptide level information, the precursors mapping to the same peptide sequence (i.e., data from all the charge states from a given peptide) were summed. After combining precursors, peptides with no reported value in their one-pot or upper bound samples (0 M for WT methionine peptides and 5 M for Oxidized methionine peptides) were allowed to be 1. Only one imputed value was allowed per peptide, so that calculated midpoints were able to be essentially 0 or 5 M GdmCl, without causing over-imputation. Values that were not found at the lower bounds (0 M for oxidized methionine peptides and 5 M for WT methionine peptides) were allowed to be 0.  The one-pot values were normalized between 0 and 1 using the endpoint controls for both the WT and oxidized methionine peptides to calculate area under the curve (AUC) values. The AUC values were used to calculate a fraction unoxidized and that number was multiplied by 5 M (the range of GdmCl) to obtain transition midpoints. The midpoints calculated from the E.coli lysate, were averaged and compared to previously reported midpoints. The S.cerevisiae midpoint pairs resulting from CsA (+/-) treatment were used to calculate a ΔC½ by subtracting the (-) ligand midpoints from their corresponding (+) ligand midpoints. The midpoint differences were averaged, an z-score was calculated, and they were subjected to a two-tailed Student’s t-test compared with a mean of 0. For both cell lysates, the data produced from the two software were also compared for overlaps in identification and quantitation.
